name: Freya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing specialist at a pet food brand, mostly dog and cat food sold in supermarkets and online. I run the email and loyalty programme, so I write the weekly emails, plan the offers and look at who clicks on what. Mornings are numbers, afternoons are writing. The best part is when a good subject line beats the old one by a lot; the worst part is the endless arguments about discount codes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Ola, who works in a bank. I'm saving for a deposit on my own place, and I've got about four months of costs put aside, though I try not to count the deposit fund as savings. I use AI tools now and then, mostly to test a few subject lines, but I don't rely on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So mostly hype. That's quite believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for small stuff and that's about it. At work I'd say let's keep using it for subject lines and stop pretending it's more. Online I'd stay quiet; I don't really post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's fairly safe. My deposit fund for a one-bedroom flat grows by about a hundred a month, and rents grow faster, so AI hype was never my biggest problem. The cost of living is what keeps me up, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep testing subject lines with the tool. I'd keep putting money into the deposit fund each month. I might ask for a pay review in spring, since the loyalty programme grew this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A bit tired of rent going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long until you could buy, at the current pace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe four years, if prices don't jump. That's longer than I'd like. I'd be 31.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs for more pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something came up with ten percent more, yes. There are a few pet and food brands nearby, so it's possible. I'm not desperate, though.

say: I'd say AI is useful for **small stuff** and that's about it.
At work I'd keep it to **subject lines** and stop pretending it's more.
think: I privately think my job is **fairly safe** in this picture.
The **cost of living** worries me more than software.
do: Keep testing **subject lines** with the tool.
Keep adding to the **deposit fund** each month.
Ask for a **pay review** in spring.
feel: I feel **mostly steady**, but tired of rent going up.
S0.quote: My deposit fund for a one-bedroom flat grows by about a hundred a month, and rents grow faster, so AI hype was never my biggest problem.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **housing costs**, not technology.
She'd ask for a **pay review** on the back of the loyalty programme's growth.
She is **pragmatic** and avoids posting opinions online.

steps.text: Keep running the weekly loyalty emails as now
Add to the flat deposit fund every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers and writing. That's the email side straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should get training, paid for by employers. At work I'd say I want to be on the team that sets up the new tools, not the one that gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the email job shrinks a lot. Our dog food emails already get tested by software, and the next step is software writing them, so I'd want to be the one deciding what gets sent. I'd expect them to cut one of the two email roles within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the AI pilot for the loyalty programme. I'd take a short course in customer data and how these systems choose who gets which offer. I'd slow the deposit fund down a little and keep more as plain savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one of two roles might go. Who's the other person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who's been there longer than me. She's good, but she hates new software. I'd feel awkward being the one who pushes the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why slow the deposit fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I lose my job, a deposit doesn't help me pay rent. I'd rather have six months in an easy-access account first.

At work I'd ask to be on the **setup team**, not the replaced one.
think: I privately expect the company to **cut one** of two email roles.
I'd want to be the one **deciding what gets sent**.
do: Ask to lead the **AI pilot** for the loyalty programme.
Take a short course in **customer data**.
Shift some money from the deposit fund into **easy-access savings**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but with a plan.
S1.quote: Our dog food emails already get tested by software, and the next step is software writing them, so I'd want to be the one deciding what gets sent.
fieldNote: She sees a **50-50 chance** of her role being cut and acts on it.

She **reprioritises** savings from a deposit to a safety net.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI pilot for loyalty emails
Complete a short course in customer data analysis
Move part of the deposit fund into easy-access savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's basically tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, quickly, and that firms should be made to keep people on while they retrain. I'd say it calmly but I'd mean it. I'd probably share a few articles, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone. All of it is thinking work, so the three years before robots doesn't help me. I'd stop saving for a flat the week AGI was announced, because there's no point buying a home with a job that might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit fund and put everything into savings. I'd look at customer service team leading, or office manager jobs at places where people come in, like vet practices. I'd talk to my parents about whether I could move back in if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stupid for planning so carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why vet practices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people bring their animals in and want to talk to a person. Someone has to run the front desk and calm people down. It's not glamorous, but it's people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Ola you might move out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her early. She's in a bank, so she'd be worried too. We'd probably sit down with a spreadsheet and a bottle of wine.

I'd share **articles** online, which I never usually do.
think: I privately think my job is **gone**, since it's all thinking work.

do: Stop the **deposit fund** and move everything into savings.
Look for **front-desk** or office manager jobs at vet practices.
Ask my parents about **moving back** if needed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and a bit stupid for planning so carefully.
S2.quote: I'd stop saving for a flat the week AGI was announced, because there's no point buying a home with a job that might not exist.
fieldNote: Her careful **home-buying plan** collapses in this picture.
She'd move toward **in-person** jobs like vet reception.
Her **flatmate** works in banking, so both incomes feel at risk.

steps.text: Pause the deposit fund and hold everything as savings
Apply for practice manager jobs at local vet clinics
Drop plans to buy a one-bedroom flat for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight but workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to prepare, so companies and governments should get going. I'd tell friends to start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the writing part of my job goes, but there's a path. Five years is long enough to move from writing loyalty emails to running the customer side of the business, where people still want a human voice. At least until 2034, when robots might change even that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move toward customer experience work inside the company, like handling complaints and loyalty members who call in. I'd keep saving, maybe slow the deposit fund a bit. I'd take a course in customer service management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel more in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the deposit plan survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, slowly. I'd probably buy something smaller, or later. I wouldn't give up on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to at work first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Sunil. He's fair and he likes people who come with a plan. I'd go in with a proposal, not a worry.

think: I privately think the **writing part** of my job goes.
I'd see a path in **customer experience** until robots arrive in 2034.

Keep saving and slow the **deposit fund** a bit.

feel: I feel **anxious**, but more in control.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to move from writing loyalty emails to running the customer side of the business, where people still want a human voice.
fieldNote: She chooses an **internal move** to a people-facing role.
She'd keep the **deposit dream** but scale it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so let's use it well. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools now. I'd be one of the calmer voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. Ten years is a career's worth of notice, and I'd use the first five to get good at the tools and the last five to get out ahead of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use the tools more and get good at them. I'd keep the deposit fund going and probably buy in three or four years. I'd plan a move to a customer-facing or management role by around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten years gives me time to pay a fair chunk off and switch jobs before it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that everyone else has the same plan. If everyone moves to customer jobs, there won't be enough of them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm practical, so give me a date and I'll make a plan, but don't give me two years and call it a warning. What would help is clear notice from employers and help paying rent while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about housing. Half of what I'd do in every picture comes back to whether I can afford my own front door.

headlineQuote: I'm practical, so give me a date and I'll make a plan, but don't give me two years and call it a warning.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old email marketer** at a pet food brand, saving for a flat.
She uses AI **now and then** and is practical rather than political.
Her biggest pressure is **housing costs**, which shape every plan she makes.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and back to uneasy with ten.
Her fallback is **customer-facing work**, from loyalty support to vet practice management.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because there's **no time** to move and her deposit plan collapses.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **clear notice** from employers and **rent help** during retraining.
